title: supplyAsync default pool — ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), why use dedicated executor in production

s1_definition.profdef: `supplyAsync()` and `runAsync()` without an executor parameter use `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` — a SHARED, JVM-wide pool with parallelism = `Runtime.availableProcessors() - 1` (e.g., 3 threads on a 4-core machine). Problems in production: (1) **Shared** — ALL CompletableFutures, parallel streams, and frameworks using commonPool compete for the same 3 threads. (2) **Small** — designed for CPU-bound tasks (cores threads). Blocking IO on these threads starves everything. (3) **No control** — can't set thread names (poor debugging), can't set daemon status, can't configure rejection policy, can't monitor. **Fix**: always pass a dedicated `ExecutorService` — separate IO pool (many threads) from CPU pool (cores threads). Named threads for debugging. Bounded queues for back-pressure.
s1_definition.analogy: `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` = the bank has ONE shared car for ALL departments. Delivery, pickup, executive travel — all share 3 cars. If delivery takes 3 cars for long trips → executives can't travel → entire bank stalled! **Dedicated executor** = each department has its OWN fleet. Delivery: 20 vans. Executive: 3 sedans. IT: 5 bikes. One department's heavy usage doesn't affect others.
s1_definition.oneliner: Default: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (shared, small, no control). Production: ALWAYS pass dedicated executor. IO pool (many threads) + CPU pool (cores). Named threads. Bounded queues.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `supplyAsync()` and `runAsync()` without an executor parameter use `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` — a SHARED, JVM-wide pool with parallelism = `Runtime.availableProcessors() - 1` (e.g., 3 threads on a 4-core machine). Problems in production: (1) **Shared** — ALL CompletableFutures, parallel streams, and frameworks using commonPool compete for the same 3 threads. (2) **Small** — designed for CPU-bound tasks (cores threads). Blocking IO on these threads starves everything. (3) **No control** — can't set thread names (poor debugging), can't set daemon status, can't configure rejection policy, can't monitor. **Fix**: always pass a dedicated `ExecutorService` — separate IO pool (many threads) from CPU pool (cores threads). Named threads for debugging. Bounded queues for back-pressure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` = the bank has ONE shared car for ALL departments. Delivery, pickup, executive travel — all share 3 cars. If delivery takes 3 cars for long trips → executives can't travel → entire bank stalled! **Dedicated executor** = each department has its OWN fleet. Delivery: 20 vans. Executive: 3 sedans. IT: 5 bikes. One department's heavy usage doesn't affect others.

**One line to remember:** Default: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (shared, small, no control). Production: ALWAYS pass dedicated executor. IO pool (many threads) + CPU pool (cores). Named threads. Bounded queues.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The payment service used default `supplyAsync()` for 100 concurrent payment gateway calls (200ms each).** ForkJoinPool had 3 threads (4-core server). 3 payments at a time → 100 payments took 7 seconds instead of 200ms. PLUS: parallel streams in the reporting service ALSO used commonPool → reports delayed because payment threads hogged all 3 workers. Fix: `paymentPool = newFixedThreadPool(50)`. `supplyAsync(callGateway, paymentPool)`. 50 threads → 100 payments in 400ms. commonPool free for reporting.
sections.s4e_build:

```bash
mvn clean test

```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 (default).** 20 IO tasks on commonPool (3 threads). Batch 1: 3 tasks (200ms). Batch 2: 3 tasks (200ms). ... Batch 7: 2 tasks. Total: ~1400ms.

**Step 2 (dedicated).** 20 IO tasks on dedicated 20-thread pool. All 20 start simultaneously. All complete in ~200ms. 7x faster!

**Step 3 (named).** Thread dump shows "payment-worker" instead of "ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1". Instant identification of which service's thread is stuck.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ DEFAULT: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() ═══

  commonPool (3 threads):
  CF.supplyAsync() ──→ ┌─worker-1─┐
  CF.supplyAsync() ──→ │ worker-2 │ ← ALL CF + parallel streams share these 3!
  CF.supplyAsync() ──→ └─worker-3─┘
  CF.supplyAsync() ──→ QUEUED! Waits for a free worker...

  ═══ DEDICATED: separate pools ═══

  ioPool (50 threads):     cpuPool (4 threads):
  payment calls ──→ 50     encryption ──→ 4
  DB queries   ──→ workers  sorting    ──→ workers

  commonPool: free for parallel streams + framework use!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Executor Segregation in Banking ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Banking Service                                  │
  │                                                    │
  │  ioPool (50 threads, named "io-worker-N"):        │
  │  ├─ Payment gateway calls                         │
  │  ├─ Credit bureau API                             │
  │  └─ DB queries                                     │
  │                                                    │
  │  cpuPool (4 threads, named "cpu-worker-N"):       │
  │  ├─ Encryption                                     │
  │  └─ Report generation                             │
  │                                                    │
  │  ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (3 threads):           │
  │  └─ parallel streams (LEFT FREE!)                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ForkJoinPool.commonPool() ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ForkJoinPool.commonPool()            │
  │  - parallelism: cores - 1            │  (3 on 4-core)
  │  - SHARED across entire JVM!          │
  │  - Used by: supplyAsync(), runAsync() │
  │  - Used by: parallelStream()          │
  │  - Used by: many frameworks           │
  │  - No named threads                   │
  │  - No bounded queue                   │
  │  - No rejection policy                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══ PRODUCTION EXECUTOR ═══
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Custom ThreadPoolExecutor            │
  │  - core: 20, max: 50                 │  sized for IO
  │  - queue: LinkedBlockingQueue(1000)  │  bounded!
  │  - threadFactory: named threads      │  "payment-worker-1"
  │  - rejection: CallerRunsPolicy       │  back-pressure!
  │  - daemon: true (optional)            │
  │  - monitoring: getActiveCount() etc.  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Rule: NEVER use commonPool for blocking IO in production!
  Always: supplyAsync(task, dedicatedPool)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`supplyAsync()` defaults to `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` — a shared, JVM-wide pool with parallelism = cores - 1. In production, this is dangerous: the pool is SHARED by all CompletableFutures, parallel streams, and many frameworks. It's SMALL — designed for CPU-bound, not IO-bound work. Blocking IO on commonPool threads starves everything in the JVM. There's NO control over thread names, queue bounds, or rejection policies.

Always pass a dedicated `ExecutorService`: `supplyAsync(task, ioPool)`. Separate IO pool (many threads, named "io-worker-N") from CPU pool (cores threads, named "cpu-worker-N"). Use bounded queues with rejection policies (CallerRunsPolicy for back-pressure). Named threads make thread dumps instantly readable. In banking: payment gateway calls (200ms blocking) on commonPool's 3 threads → 100 payments took 7 seconds. Dedicated 50-thread pool → same 100 payments in 400ms. commonPool freed for reporting parallel streams.

---

keyPoints: Blocking IO starves other tasks — use custom executor
